$
solution:
The cross-sectional area of the inflow tap be $\mathrm{A}_{\text {tap }}=\mathrm{A}$.

The speed of water emerging from the tap be $\mathrm{v}(\mathrm{t})=10\left(1-\sin \frac{\pi}{30} \mathrm{t}\right)$.

The cross-sectional area of the tank be $\mathrm{A}_{\text {tank }}=10 \mathrm{~A}$.

The volume of water entering the tank in an infinitesimal time interval dt is:

$$\mathrm{d}V = A_{\text{tap}}\,v(t)\,\mathrm{d}t = A\left[10\left(1-\sin\frac{\pi}{30}t\right)\right]\mathrm{d}t$$

Let H(t) be the height of the water level in the tank at any time t. The increase in water volume inside the tank during time dt is:

$$\mathrm{d}V = A_{\text{tank}}\,\mathrm{d}H = 10\mathrm{d}H$$

$$10\,\mathrm{d}H = 10\left(1-\sin\frac{\pi}{30}t\right)\mathrm{d}t$$

$$\mathrm{d}H = \left(1-\sin\frac{\pi}{30}t\right)\mathrm{d}t$$

At $t=0$, the tank is empty, so $H(0)=0$. Integrating both sides from $t=0$ to $t=15\ \text{s}$,

$$H = \int\limits_{0}^{15} \left(1-\sin\frac{\pi}{30}t\right)\mathrm{d}t$$

$$H = \int\limits_{0}^{15} \mathrm{d}t + \int\limits_{0}^{15} \left(\sin\frac{\pi}{30}t\right)\mathrm{d}t = [t]_{0}^{15} + \frac{30}{\pi}\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{30}t\right)$$

$$H = t + \frac{30}{\pi}\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{30}t\right) = \left[t + \frac{30}{\pi}\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{30}t\right)\right]_{0}^{15}$$

$$H = \left[15-\frac{30}{\pi}\left[\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{30}\times 15\right)-\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{30}\times 0\right)\right]\right]\ \text{m}$$

$$H = \left[15-\frac{30}{\pi}\left[\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right)-0\right]\right]\ \text{m}$$

$$ \mathrm{H}=\left[15-\frac{30}{\pi}\right] \mathrm{m} $$

Therefore, the correct option is (D).

question: A container filled with liquid up to height h is placed on smooth horizontal surface. The container is having a small hole at the bottom. As the liquid comes out from the hole, the container moves in a backward direction with small acceleration a and finally, when all the liquid is drained out, it acquires velocity v0. Neglect mass of the container. In this case,
options: both a and v0 depend on h
neither a nor v0 depend on h
solution:
Let the cross-sectional area of the container be $\mathrm{A}_0$.

The container be filled with a liquid of density $\rho$ up to an instantaneous height $y$ (initially $y=h$ ).

The area of the small opening at the bottom be $\mathrm{a}_0\left(\mathrm{a}_0 \ll \mathrm{~A}_0\right)$.

Using Bernoulli's equation, the velocity of the liquid exiting horizontally through the hole relative to the container is

$$ \mathrm{P}_0+\rho $\mathrm{gy}=\mathrm{P}$_0+\frac{1}{2} \rho \mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{rel}}^2 \Rightarrow \mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{rel}}=\sqrt{2 \mathrm{gy}} $$

The mass flow rate of the escaping liquid is

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}m_{\text{out}}}{\mathrm{d}t}=\rho\,a_0\,v_{\text{rel}}=\rho\,a_0\sqrt{2gy}$$

The mass escaping the container will have linear momentum, $\Delta p=m_{\text{out}}v_{\text{rel}}$

Using Newton’s second law of motion the backward thrust force $F_{\text{thrust}}$ exerted on the container is,

$$F_{\text{thrust}}=\frac{\mathrm{d}p}{\mathrm{d}t}=v_{\text{rel}}\frac{\mathrm{d}m_{\text{out}}}{\mathrm{d}t}=\left(\sqrt{2gy}\right)\left(\rho\,a_0\sqrt{2gy}\right)=2\rho\,a_0\,g\,y$$

The container is on a smooth horizontal surface, and its own mass is negligible. Therefore, the total mass of the system at that instant is the mass of the remaining liquid, $M(y)=\rho A_0 y$

Using Newton's second law, the backward acceleration $a$ of the container at any instant is

$$a=\frac{F_{\text{thrust}}}{M(y)}=\frac{2\rho\,a_0\,g\,y}{\rho A_0 y}=\frac{2a_0g}{A_0}$$

Since $a_0$, $A_0$, and $g$ are constants, the acceleration $a$ is independent of the height $h$.

The time rate of decrease of liquid level inside the container is,

$$A_0\left(-\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}t}\right)=a_0\,v_{\text{rel}}=a_0\sqrt{2gy}$$

$$\mathrm{d}t=-\frac{A_0}{a_0\sqrt{2g}}\,y^{-1/2}\,\mathrm{d}y$$

Since acceleration is $a=\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}t}$, the total velocity change from the initial state $(t=0, y=h)$ to the instant when all liquid is drained $(y=0)$ is:

$$\mathrm{d}v=a\,\mathrm{d}t=\left(\frac{2a_0g}{A_0}\right)\left(-\frac{A_0}{a_0\sqrt{2g}}y^{-1/2}\,\mathrm{d}y\right)=-\sqrt{2g}\,y^{-1/2}\,\mathrm{d}y$$

Integrating from $y=h$ to $y=0$:

$$v_0=\int\limits_h^{0}-\sqrt{2g}\,y^{-1/2}\,\mathrm{d}y=-\sqrt{2g}\int\limits_h^{0}y^{-1/2}\,\mathrm{d}y$$

$$v_0=\sqrt{2g}\left[2\sqrt{y}\right]_{0}^{h}=2\sqrt{2gh}$$

The final velocity $v_0$ is proportional to $\sqrt{h}$, which means $v_0$ directly depends on the height $h$.

Thus, the acceleration $\mathrm{a}=\frac{2 \mathrm{a}_0 \mathrm{~g}}{\mathrm{~A}_0}$ does not depend on h and the final velocity $\mathrm{v}_0=2 \sqrt{2 \mathrm{gh}}$ does depend on h.

Therefore, only $\mathrm{v}_0$ depends on h. Hence, the correct option is (C).

question: A wide vessel and a tube is connected as shown in the figure. Water is filled inside vessel and tube. When tube is opened the water flows out as shown in the figure. The pressure at point P, at mid point of tube is (cross section of the tube is very-very small)
solution:
According to Bernoulli's equation $\mathrm{P}+\frac{1}{2} \rho \mathrm{v}^2+\rho \mathrm{gh}=$ constant.

Here, P is the static pressure, v is the flow velocity and y is the vertical elevation above a chosen reference line.

The upper vessel has liquid filled up to height H , and the narrow tube extending downwards has total length 2 H .

Therefore, the top open surface of the water in the wide vessel is at elevation, $\mathrm{y}_{\text {top }}=2 \mathrm{H}+\mathrm{H}=3 \mathrm{H}$

Point P is at the midpoint of the lower tube. Therefore, the elevation of point P is $\mathrm{y}_{\mathrm{P}}=\mathrm{H}$

Both the top surface of the vessel and the exit of the tube are open to the atmosphere, so their static pressures are equal to atmospheric pressure $\mathrm{P}_0$.

The area of the wide vessel $\mathrm{A}_{\text {vessel }}$ is extremely large compared to the cross-sectional area of the narrow tube $\mathrm{a}_{\text {tube }}, \frac{\mathrm{a}_{\text {tube }}}{\mathrm{A}_{\text {vessel }}} \rightarrow 0$

By the continuity equation $\left(A_{\text {vessel }} v_{\text {top }}=a_{\text {tube }} v_{\text {exit }}\right)$, the fluid velocity at the top surface is negligible.

$$ \mathrm{v}_{\text {top }} \approx 0 $$

Applying Bernoulli's equation between the top open surface ($y_{\text{top}} = 3H$) and the exit of the tube ($y_{\text{exit}} = 0$),

$$P_0 + 0 + \rho g (3H) = P_0 + \frac{1}{2}\rho v_{\text{exit}}^2 + 0$$

$$\frac{1}{2}\rho v_{\text{exit}}^2 = 3\rho g H$$

The narrow tube has uniform cross-section throughout its length from the bottom of the vessel to the exit.

By the continuity equation, the flow velocity inside the tube is constant everywhere along the tube:

$$v_P = v_{\text{exit}}$$

$$\Rightarrow \frac{1}{2}\rho v_P^2 = \frac{1}{2}\rho v_{\text{exit}}^2 = 3\rho g H$$

Using Bernoulli's equation between point P ($y_P = H$) and the exit ($y_{\text{exit}} = 0$),

$$P_P + \frac{1}{2}\rho v_P^2 + \rho g y_P = P_{\text{exit}} + \frac{1}{2}\rho v_{\text{exit}}^2 + \rho g y_{\text{exit}}$$

$$P_P + \rho g H = P_0 + 0$$

$$P_P = P_0 - \rho g H$$

Therefore, the pressure at point P is $P_0 - \rho g H$. Thus, the correct option is (D).

solution:
For an incompressible fluid, the density $\rho$ is constant.

The mass $\Delta \mathrm{m}$ entering the inlet in a small time interval $\Delta \mathrm{t}$ is $\Delta \mathrm{m}_{\mathrm{in}}=\rho \cdot \Delta \mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{in}}$

The volume of fluid entering through cross-sectional area $\mathrm{A}_1$ with speed $\mathrm{v}_1$ in time $\Delta \mathrm{t}$ is the volume of a cylinder of base area $\mathrm{A}_1$ and length $\Delta \mathrm{x}_1=\mathrm{v}_1 \Delta \mathrm{t}$.

$$ \Delta \mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{in}}=\mathrm{A}_1 \mathrm{v}_1 \Delta \mathrm{t} $$

Therefore, the incoming mass rate (mass per unit time) is

$$\frac{dm_{\mathrm{in}}}{dt} = \rho A_1 v_1$$

Similarly, the liquid leaves through two branches with cross-sectional areas $A_2$ and $A_3$, moving with speeds $v_2$ and $v_3$ respectively. The outgoing mass rate is,

$$\frac{dm_{\mathrm{out}}}{dt} = \rho A_2 v_2 + \rho A_3 v_3$$

Because the liquid is incompressible, mass cannot accumulate at the junction

$$\frac{dm_{\mathrm{in}}}{dt} = \frac{dm_{\mathrm{out}}}{dt}$$

$$\rho A_1 v_1 = \rho A_2 v_2 + \rho A_3 v_3 \Rightarrow A_1 v_1 = A_2 v_2 + A_3 v_3$$

The cross-sectional area of main inlet branch is $A_1 = A$ and the liquid is flow speed $v_1 = 3.0\ \mathrm{m/s}$

The cross-sectional area of first outlet branch is $A_2 = A$ and the liquid is flow speed $v_2 = 1.5\ \mathrm{m/s}$

The cross-sectional area of second outlet branch is $A_3 = A$.

We need to find the speed of liquid flow through third outlet.

$$A(3.0) = A(1.5) + (1.5A)v \Rightarrow 3.0 = 1.5 + 1.5v$$

$$1.5 = 1.5v \Rightarrow v = \frac{1.5}{1.5} = 1.0\ \text{m/s}$$

Therefore, the correct option is (C).

question: Fountains usually seen in gardens are generated by a wide pipe with an enclosure at one end having many small holes. Consider one such fountain which is produced by a pipe of internal diameter 2 cm in which water flows at a rate $3 \ \mathrm\mathrm\mathrm\mathrm\mathrm{ms}^{-1}$. The enclosure has 100 holes each of diameter 0.05 cm. The velocity of water coming out of the holes is (in $\mathrm\mathrm\mathrm\mathrm\mathrm{ms}^{-1}$)
solution:
Assuming water as an ideal, incompressible fluid, using conservation of mass, the total volume of fluid entering the pipe per unit time must equal the total volume of fluid exiting through all the holes per unit time.

Let $A_{\text{pipe}}$ be the cross-sectional area of the main delivery pipe and $v_{\text{pipe}}$ be the flow speed of water in the pipe.

$N=100$ be the total number of identical small holes whose cross-sectional area of single hole is $a_{\text{hole}}$.

For circular cross-sections of diameter $D$ and $d$

$$A_{\text{pipe}}=\frac{\pi D^2}{4};\ a_{\text{hole}}=\frac{\pi d^2}{4}$$

The velocity of water exiting each hole is $v$.

The total volume entering the pipe per second is

$$Q_{\text{in}}=A_{\text{pipe}}\,v_{\text{pipe}}$$

The total volume exiting through $N$ holes per second is,

$$Q_{\text{out}}=N\cdot a_{\text{hole}}\cdot v$$

Using the continuity equation the input and output volume flow rates ($Q_{\text{in}}=Q_{\text{out}}$):

$$A_{\text{pipe}}v_{\text{pipe}}=Na_{\text{hole}}v$$

$$\left(\frac{\pi D^2}{4}\right)v_{\text{pipe}}=N\left(\frac{\pi d^2}{4}\right)v$$

$$D^2v_{\text{pipe}}=Nd^2v$$

$$v = \frac{D^2 v_{\text{pipe}}}{N d^2} = \frac{v_{\text{pipe}}}{N} \left(\frac{D}{d}\right)^2$$

Internal diameter of the pipe, $D = 2\ \text{cm}$

Flow velocity in the pipe, $v_{\text{pipe}} = 3\ \text{m/s}$

Number of holes, $N = 100$

Diameter of each hole, $d = 0.05\ \text{cm}$

Putting the values, $$v = \frac{3}{100} \left(\frac{2}{0.05}\right)^2 = \frac{3}{100} \times 1600 \Rightarrow v = 3 \times 16 = 48\ \text{m/s}$$

Therefore, the correct option is (D).

question: As shown in the figure water squirts horizontally out of two small holes in the side of the cylinder and the two streams strike the ground at the same point. If hole Q is at a height h above ground and level of water stands to a height H, then the height of P above ground level is
solution:
A large open cylinder with total water level at a height H measured from the ground.

Let a small hole be situated at a height $y$ above the ground.

The depth of this hole below the top free water surface is $d = H - y$

Applying Bernoulli's theorem the horizontal efflux speed is $v = \sqrt{2gd} = \sqrt{2g(H - y)}$

After exiting horizontally, the water drops freely from height $y$ to the ground under gravity $(g)$.

If the time of flight is $t$, then using kinematic equation $[s = ut + \frac{1}{2}at^2]$

$$y = \frac{1}{2}gt^2 \Rightarrow t = \sqrt{2yg}$$

$$ P_{\mathrm{atm}}+\rho \mathrm{g} \mathrm{H}_{\mathrm{eff}}+\frac{1}{2} \rho v_{\mathrm{surface}}^2=P_{\mathrm{atm}}+\frac{1}{2} \rho v^2 $$

Let $\mathrm{P}_0$ be the atmospheric pressure of the surrounding stationary air.

When air is blown horizontally across the open top surface of the tank with a speed $u_{\text{air}}$, Using Bernoulli's principle to the moving air,

$$P_{\text{top}} + \frac{1}{2}\rho_{\text{air}}\,u_{\text{air}}^2 = P_0$$

$$P_{\text{top}} = P_0 - \frac{1}{2}\rho_{\text{air}}\,u_{\text{air}}^2$$

Since $u_{\text{air}} > 0$, the pressure directly above the water surface decreases below atmospheric pressure.

$$P_{\text{top}} < P_0$$

The density of the water in the tank is $\rho$ and the depth of hole below the top water surface is $h$.

Point 1 is at the top surface inside the tank where pressure is $P_{\text{top}}$ and the downward velocity of the large surface is negligible ($v_1 \approx 0$) because the cross-sectional area of hole is very small compared to that of container.

Point 2 be just outside the hole, where the water jet is exposed to the stationary atmosphere, so $P_2 = P_0$.

Let the speed of efflux is $v$.

$$P_{\text{top}} + \rho gh + 0 = P_0 + \frac{1}{2}\rho\,v^2$$

$$\frac{1}{2}\rho\,v^2 = \rho gh + (P_{\text{top}} - P_0)$$

The water travels vertically upward through the hydrant and then does $90^\circ$ turn to emerge horizontally at speed $v$. The pipe and nozzle have uniform cross-section throughout. The force exerted by the water on the corner of the hydrant is
solution:
Let the fluid have density $\rho$ and volume flow rate L .

The mass flowing through the hydrant per unit time is, $\frac{\mathrm{dm}}{\mathrm{dt}}=\rho \mathrm{L}$

Since the pipe and nozzle have a uniform cross-section throughout, the magnitude of the velocity remains constant at speed v.

The initial vertical upward flow is along the $+\hat{\jmath}$ direction $\vec{v}_{\text {in }}=v \hat{\jmath}$

The final horizontal flow after a $90^\circ$ turn is along the $+\hat{i}$ direction, $\vec{v}_{\text{out}} = v\hat{i}$

The net change in velocity per unit volume of water is,

$$\Delta \vec{v} = \vec{v}_{\text{out}} - \vec{v}_{\text{in}} = v\hat{i} - v\hat{j}$$

By Newton's second law, the net force exerted by the hydrant walls on the turning water is the rate of change of momentum of the fluid,

$$\vec{F}_W = \frac{\mathrm{d}m}{\mathrm{d}t}\left[(\vec{v}_{\text{out}} - \vec{v}_{\text{in}})\right] = (\rho\,L)(v\hat{i} - v\hat{j}) = \rho\,v\,L\,\hat{i} - \rho\,v\,L\,\hat{j}$$

By Newton's third law of motion (action and reaction), the force exerted by the water on the corner of the hydrant is equal in magnitude and opposite in direction,

$$\vec{F}_H = -\vec{F}_W = -\rho\,v\,L\,\hat{i} + \rho\,v\,L\,\hat{j}$$

So, the magnitude of this force is

$$F = |\vec{F}_H| = \sqrt{(-\rho\,v\,L)^2 + (\rho\,v\,L)^2} = \sqrt{2(\rho\,v\,L)^2} = \sqrt{2}\,\rho\,v\,L$$

Thus, the correct option is (D).

$
solution:
The stream flow horizontally with uniform speed $\mathrm{v}=2 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$ at a depth h below the free surface of the water stream.

Atmospheric pressure be $\mathrm{P}_0$.

The upper closed end of the tube is at a height $\mathrm{h}_0=10 \mathrm{~cm}=0.1 \mathrm{~m}$ above the free water surface.

A small orifice is at the top closed surface of the tube.

The water jet spurt vertically upward through the orifice to a maximum height $\mathrmh^{\prime}$.

At point 1 is in the stream at depth $h$ below the free water surface,

Pressure $\mathrm{P}_1=\mathrm{P}_0+\rho \mathrm{gh}$

Velocity is $\mathrm{v}_1=\mathrm{v}$

Height relative to the free water surface is $y_1=-h$

At point 2 is in the stream at depth $h_0$ at the water surface,

The water emerges into the atmosphere, so the pressure at the jet is atmospheric $P_2=P_0$

Velocity of water exiting the orifice is $v_2=v_{\text{jet}}$

Height relative to the free water surface is $y_2=-h_0$

Height relative to the free water surface: $y_2=+h_0$

Using Bernoulli's equation from stream (point 1) to orifice (point 2),

$$P_1+\frac{1}{2}\rho v_1^2+\rho g y_1=P_2+\frac{1}{2}\rho v_2^2+\rho g y_2$$

$$\left(P_0+\rho g h\right)+\frac{1}{2}\rho v^2+\rho g(-h)=P_0+\frac{1}{2}\rho v_{\text{jet}}^2+\rho g h_0$$

$$\frac{1}{2}\rho v^2=\frac{1}{2}\rho v_{\text{jet}}^2+\rho g h_0$$

$$v^2=v_{\text{jet}}^2+2gh_0$$

$$v_{\text{jet}}^2=v^2-2gh_0$$

Once the water emerges vertically from the orifice with initial upward speed $v_{\text{jet}}$, it rises under gravity until its vertical velocity becomes zero at the maximum height $h'$.

Using the kinematic equation for vertical motion under gravity ($v_{\text{top}}^2=v_{\text{jet}}^2-2gh'$ with $v_{\text{top}}=0$):

$$0=v_{\text{jet}}^2-2gh' \Rightarrow h'=\frac{v_{\text{jet}}^2}{2g}$$

$$h'=\frac{v^2-2gh_0}{2g}=\frac{v^2}{2g}-h_0$$

The velocity of stream is $v=2\ \text{m/s}$

Height of upper end above surface is $\mathrm{h}_0=10 \mathrm{~cm}=0.1 \mathrm{~m}$

Acceleration due to gravity is $\mathrm{g}=10 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^2$

Substituting these values,

$$ \frac{\mathrm{v}^2}{2 \mathrm{~g}}=\frac{(2)^2}{2 \times 10}=\frac{4}{20}=0.2 \mathrm{~m}=20 \mathrm{~cm} $$

Therefore, the height $\mathrmh^{\prime}$ is $\mathrmh^{\prime}=20 \mathrm{~cm}-10 \mathrm{~cm}=10 \mathrm{~cm} \Rightarrow \mathrm{n}=10$

Therefore, the value of n is 10 .

The water level falls by $\lambda \mathrm{m} / \mathrm{s}$ and the shape of the jar is given by $\mathrm{y} \propto \mathrmx^{\mathrm{n}}$. question: The shape of an ancient water clock jar is such that the water level descends at a constant rate at all times. The water level falls by $\lambda \mathrm{m} / \mathrm{s}$ and the shape of the jar is given by $\mathrm{y} \propto \mathrmx^{\mathrm{n}}$. Find the value of n if the radius $\mathbf{r}$ of the drain hole can be assumed to be very small.
solution:
A container with a small drain hole of radius r located at the bottom $(\mathrm{y}=0)$.

The area of the drain hole is $\mathrm{a}_0=\pi \mathrm{r}^2$

Let y be the instantaneous height of the water level above the drain hole.

Since the area of the drain hole $a_0$ is very small compared to the cross-sectional area of the jar at the water surface, the efflux velocity $v_{\mathrm{efflux}}$ of water leaving through the hole is,

$$v_{\mathrm{efflux}} = \sqrt{2gy}$$

Let the jar be symmetric about the vertical $y$-axis, so that the horizontal cross-section of the water surface at height $y$ is circular with radius $x$.

The cross-sectional area of the water surface at height $y$ is $A(y) = \pi x^2$

Using the equation of continuity for incompressible fluids, rate of volume outflow through drain hole is equal to the rate of volume change (decrease) inside the jar.

$$a_0\, v_{\mathrm{efflux}} = -A(y)\, \frac{dy}{dt}$$

The water level descends at a constant rate $\lambda$ m/s, $-\frac{dy}{dt} = \lambda$

Substituting $-\frac{dy}{dt} = \lambda$ and the expressions for areas and efflux velocity,

$$\Rightarrow (\pi r^2)\sqrt{2gy} = (\pi x^2)\lambda \Rightarrow r^2\sqrt{2gy} = \lambda x^2$$

$$\Rightarrow r^4(2gy) = \lambda^2 x^4 \Rightarrow y = \left(\frac{\lambda^2}{2gr^4}\right)x^4$$

Since $\lambda$, $g$, and $r$ are constants, the term $\left(\frac{\lambda^2}{2gr^4}\right)$ is a constant. Thus $y \propto x^4$

$$\Rightarrow y \propto x^n \Rightarrow n = 4$$

Therefore, the value of $n$ is 4.

question: For the arrangement shown in the figure, find the time interval in seconds after which the water jet ceases to cross the wall. solution:
The orifice is at the wall of height 1 m and width 1 m .

The jet emerges horizontally and must clear the horizontal top of the wall of width $\mathrm{X}=1 \mathrm{~m}$ while falling vertically by no more than $\mathrm{Y}=1 \mathrm{~m}$ to reach ground level.

The vertical motion of the jet is under free fall.

$$Y = \frac{1}{2}gt^2 \Rightarrow 1 = \frac{1}{2}(10)t^2 \Rightarrow t^2 = \frac{1}{5} \Rightarrow t = \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\ \mathrm{s}$$

Let h be the depth of the water level in the tank above the orifice. By Torricelli's theorem, the horizontal efflux velocity is, $v = \sqrt{2gh}$

For the stream to clear the wall of width X = 1 m, the horizontal distance traveled in time t must satisfy

$$R = v \cdot t \geq 1\ \mathrm{m}$$

$$\sqrt{2gh} \cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} = 1$$

$$\frac{2gh}{5} = 1 \Rightarrow \frac{2(10)h}{5} = 1 \Rightarrow 4h = 1 \Rightarrow h = \frac{1}{4} = 0.25\ \text{m}$$

Thus, the jet ceases to clear the wall when the water level above the orifice drops from the initial height $x_1 = 0.81\ \text{m}$ to the critical height $x_2 = 0.25\ \text{m}$.

At any instant when the water height above the orifice is $h$, by the equation of continuity.

$$-A\frac{\mathrm{d}h}{\mathrm{d}t} = av = a\sqrt{2gh}$$

$$\mathrm{d}t = -\frac{A}{a\sqrt{2g}} h^{-1/2}\, \mathrm{d}h$$

The time interval to fall the water surface from $h_1 = 0.81\ \text{m}$ to $h_2 = 0.25\ \text{m}$.

$$T = \int\limits_{0}^{T} \mathrm{d}t = -\frac{A}{a\sqrt{2g}} \int\limits_{0.81}^{0.25} h^{-1/2}\, \mathrm{d}h = \frac{2A}{a\sqrt{2g}} (\sqrt{0.81} - \sqrt{0.25})$$

$$T = \frac{2A}{a\sqrt{2g}} (0.9 - 0.5) = \frac{2A}{a\sqrt{2g}} (0.4) = \frac{0.8A}{a\sqrt{2g}}$$

The area of cross-section of tank is $A = \sqrt{5}\ \text{m}^2$ and that of hole is $a = 32\ \text{cm}^2 = 32 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{m}^2$

$$T = \frac{0.8 \times \sqrt{5}}{(32 \times 10^{-4}) \times (\sqrt{2} \times 10)} = \frac{0.8 \times \sqrt{5}}{(32 \times 10^{-4}) \times (2\sqrt{5})}$$

$$T = \frac{0.8}{64 \times 10^{-4}} = \frac{0.8 \times 10^4}{64} = \frac{8000}{64} = 125\ \text{s}$$

Therefore, the time interval after which the water jet ceases to cross the wall is $125\ \text{s}$.

A small hole of area of cross-section $\mathbf{a}=\sqrt{\mathbf{6}} \mathbf{~ c m}^{\mathbf{2}}$ is made at height $\frac{\mathbf{h}}{\mathbf{2}}$ from the bottom. Find the area of cross-section (in $\mathbf{c m}^{\mathbf{2}}$ ) of stream of liquid just before it hits the ground.
question: A fixed cylindrical tank having large cross-section area is filled with two liquids of densities $\rho$ and $2 \rho$ and in equal volumes as shown in the figure. A small hole of area of cross-section $\mathbf{a}=\sqrt{\mathbf{6}} \mathbf{~ c m}^{\mathbf{2}}$ is made at height $\frac{\mathbf{h}}{\mathbf{2}}$ from the bottom. Find the area of cross-section (in $\mathbf{c m}^{\mathbf{2}}$ ) of stream of liquid just before it hits the ground.
solution:
Let $\mathrm{P}_0$ be the atmospheric pressure at the open top surface of the tank.

The tank is filled with two immiscible liquid layers, each of height h .

The upper layer has density $\rho$ extending from height $\mathrm{y}=2 \mathrm{~h}$ to $\mathrm{y}=\mathrm{h}$.

The lower layer has density $2 \rho$ extending from height $\mathrm{y}=\mathrm{h}$ to $\mathrm{y}=0$.

The hole is in the side wall at a height $\frac{\mathrm{h}}{2}$ from the bottom.

The pressure at the interface between the two liquids $(y = h)$ is

$$P_2 = P_0 + ho g h$$

The depth of the hole below this interface is

$$ riangle y = h - \frac{h}{2} = \frac{h}{2}$$

Since the hole is in the liquid of density $2\rho$, the static pressure inside the tank at the level of the hole is

$$P_{\text{hole}} = P_2 + (2\rho)g\left(\frac{h}{2}\right) = (P_0 + \rho g h) + \rho g h = P_0 + 2\rho g h$$

Using the Bernoulli’s principle between points 3 and 4.

$$P_{\text{hole}} + 0 = P_0 + \frac{1}{2}(2\rho)v_1^2$$

$$(P_0 + 2\rho g h) = P_0 + \rho v_1^2$$

$$2\rho g h = \rho v_1^2 \Rightarrow v_1^2 = 2gh \Rightarrow v_1 = \sqrt{2gh}$$

The water emerges horizontally with speed $v_{1x} = v_1 = \sqrt{2gh}$ and initial vertical speed $v_{1y} = 0$.

The hole is at a vertical height

$$H = \frac{h}{2}$$

above the ground. As the liquid falls freely under gravity, its horizontal velocity remains constant, $v_x = v_1 = \sqrt{2gh}$

The downward vertical velocity acquired when falling through a vertical distance $\frac{h}{2}$ is,

$$v_y^2 = 0 + 2g\left(\frac{h}{2}\right) = gh$$

The total magnitude of the velocity $v_2$ just before impact is,

$$v_2 = \sqrt{v_x^2 + v_y^2} = \sqrt{2gh + gh} = \sqrt{3gh}$$

Using the equation of continuity along the continuous stream of liquid,

$$ a_1 v_1=a_2 v_2 $$

where $\mathrm{a}_1=\mathrm{a}=\sqrt{6} \mathrm{~cm}^2$ is the initial cross-sectional area of the hole, and $\mathrm{a}_2$ is the cross-sectional area of the stream just before hitting the ground.

$$ a_2=a_1\left(\frac{v_1}{v_2}\right)=\sqrt{6} \times \frac{\sqrt{2 g h}}{\sqrt{3 g h}}=\sqrt{6} \times \sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}=\sqrt{6 \times \frac{2}{3}}=\sqrt{4}=2 \mathrm{~cm}^2 $$

Therefore, the area of cross-section of the stream just before it hits the ground is $2 \mathrm{~cm}^2$.

question:
Water filled in an empty tank of area 60 A through a tap of cross-sectional area A . The speed of water flowing out of tap is given by

$\mathbf{v}(\mathbf{m} / \mathbf{s})=\mathbf{1 0}\left[\mathbf{4}-\boldsymbol{\pi} \boldsymbol{\operatorname { s i n }} \frac{\boldsymbol{\pi}}{\mathbf{3 0}} \left(\mathbfs^{-\mathbf{1}}\right) \mathbf{t}\right]$. Find the level of water (in $\mathbf{m}$ ) in tank at $\mathrm{t}=15 \mathrm{~s}.

$
solution:
The horizontal cross-sectional area of the tank is $\mathrm{A}_{\text {tank }}=60 \mathrm{~A}$

The cross-sectional area of the tap is $\mathrm{A}_{\text {tap }}=\mathrm{A}$

The speed of water entering from the tap at time $t$ is $v(t)=10\left[4-\pi \sin \frac{\pi}{30}\left(s^{-1}\right) t\right]$ in $m / s$.

Let $H(t)$ be the height of the water level in the tank at time $t$.

The volume of water entering the tank in an infinitesimal time interval $dt$ is,

$$dV = Q_{\mathrm{in}}\,dt = A_{\mathrm{tap}}\,v(t)\,dt = A\,v(t)\,dt\ \ldots\ (i)$$

This volume causes the water level in the tank to rise by an amount $dH$,

$$dV = A_{\mathrm{tank}}\,dH = (60A)\,dH\ \ldots\ (ii)$$

From both the equations,

$$60A \, dH = A\, v(t)\, dt$$

$$\Rightarrow dH = \frac{v(t)}{60}\, dt$$

The tank is initially empty at $t = 0$, so $H(0) = 0$.

To find the water level $H$ at $t = 15\ \text{s}$.

$$H = \frac{1}{60} \int\limits_{0}^{15} v(t)\, dt$$

$$H = \frac{1}{60} \int\limits_{0}^{15} 10\left[4 - \pi \sin\left(\frac{\pi}{30}t\right)\right] dt$$

$$H = \frac{10}{60} \int\limits_{0}^{15} \left[4 - \pi \sin\left(\frac{\pi}{30}t\right)\right] dt = \frac{1}{6} \left[ \int\limits_{0}^{15} 4\, dt - \pi \int\limits_{0}^{15} \sin\left(\frac{\pi t}{30}\right) dt \right]$$

$$H = = \frac{1}{6} \left[4 \times [t]_{0}^{15} - \pi \left[-\frac{\cos\left(\frac{\pi t}{30}\right)}{\pi/30}\right]_{0}^{15}\right]$$

$$H = \frac{1}{6} \left[4 \times (15 - 0) - \frac{30}{\pi} \times \pi \left[\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right) - \cos(0)\right]\right]$$

$$H = \frac{1}{6} [60 + 30[0 - 1]] = \frac{1}{6} \times [60 - 30] = \frac{1}{6} \times 30 = 5$$

Therefore, the level of water in the tank at $t = 15\ \text{s}$ is $5\ \text{m}$.
